title: Arrays, Lists, Stacks & Queues
summary: The linear data structures everything else is built on: how arrays sit in memory, mutable and immutable string representations, linked lists and their pointer tricks, stacks, queues, deques and a first look at priority queues.

lessons.title: Arrays and memory
lessons.summary: Why arrays give O(1) indexing, how contiguous memory and CPU caches make them fast, and how dynamic arrays like Python's list, Java's ArrayList and C++'s vector grow.
lessons.body:
An **array** is the simplest data structure there is: a fixed number of same-sized slots laid out one after another in memory. Almost every other structure in this course is either built on arrays or defined by how it differs from one.

Two properties make arrays special:

- **Contiguous layout.** Element `i+1` sits immediately after element `i`. There are no gaps and no pointers between them.
- **Uniform element size.** Every slot is the same number of bytes, so the machine can compute where any element lives.

Everything good about arrays (instant indexing, cache-friendliness) and everything bad (expensive inserts, fixed size) follows from those two facts.

## Indexing is arithmetic

If an array starts at address `base` and each element takes `size` bytes, element `i` lives at:

```
address(i) = base + i * size
```

That is one multiply and one add, whatever the array's length. This is why indexing is **O(1)**: the CPU does not walk to element `i`, it calculates where it is.

```
int32 array, base = 1000, size = 4

index:    0     1     2     3     4
        +-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+
        |  7  | 12  |  3  | 40  |  9  |
        +-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+
addr:   1000  1004  1008  1012  1016
```

This also explains why most languages start indexing at **0**: the index is an *offset* from the start. Element 0 is zero elements past `base`.

> [!note] O(1) access, O(n) search
> Indexing by position is O(1). Finding a *value* in an unsorted array is still O(n), because you must look at each slot. If the array is sorted, binary search finds a value in O(log n).

## Why contiguous memory is fast

Both indexed access and a single pointer load are constant-time operations in the usual RAM model. Their measured latencies can differ because that model abstracts away the memory hierarchy.

CPUs do not fetch single bytes from RAM. They fetch a **cache line**, typically 64 bytes, and keep it in a small, fast cache. A cache hit can be much faster than a main-memory access; latency depends on hardware, contention and access pattern.

> [!note] Evidence gap
> Universal nanosecond latency figures are omitted because no measured hardware configuration or reproducible benchmark is provided.

When you scan an array, one cache line brings in sixteen 4-byte integers at once. The hardware **prefetcher** also spots the sequential pattern and loads the next lines before you ask. This is **spatial locality**, and it is why a simple loop over an array is one of the fastest things a computer can do.

A linked list (lesson 3) scatters its nodes around the heap. Each step can be a cache miss. Same O(n) on paper; often several times slower in practice.

### 2D arrays: row-major order

A rectangular built-in C or C++ array is contiguous and row-major: row 0 first, then row 1. A newly created C-order NumPy array has this layout too; NumPy also supports other strides and orders. Java int[][] is an array of references to separate int[] rows, which may have different lengths. Fortran, MATLAB and R normally use column-major layout.

```
grid (3 x 4), row-major:

[r0c0 r0c1 r0c2 r0c3 r1c0 r1c1 ...]

address(r, c) = base + (r * cols + c) * size
```

Loop order matters. Iterating row by row walks memory sequentially. Iterating column by column jumps `cols * size` bytes every step, potentially touching a different cache line each time when that stride is large. Performance depends on dimensions, cache hierarchy and compiler transformations.

## Operations and their cost

| Operation | Cost | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Read/write `a[i]` | O(1) | Address arithmetic |
| Search (unsorted) | O(n) | Check every slot |
| Insert/delete at end | O(1)* | No shifting |
| Insert/delete at `i` | O(n − i + 1) without resizing | Shift the tail; reallocation may add O(n) |

*For a dynamic array, amortised; see below.

Inserting at position `i` means shifting every later element one slot right to make room. Inserting at the front of a million-element array moves a million elements.

```python
a = [10, 20, 30, 40]
a.insert(1, 15)   # shifts 20, 30, 40 right
print(a)          # [10, 15, 20, 30, 40]
```

## Static vs dynamic arrays

A **fixed-size array** has a size chosen when it is created; this is distinct from static storage duration. C's `int a[100]` and Java's `new int[100]` are static: you cannot append a 101st element.

A **dynamic array** (resizable array) wraps a static array and tracks two numbers:

- **length**: how many elements are in use.
- **capacity**: how many slots the underlying array has.

When `length == capacity` and you append, it allocates a bigger array, copies everything across, and frees the old one.

```
capacity 4, length 4: full
[ a | b | c | d ]

append e -> allocate 8, copy, add e
[ a | b | c | d | e |   |   |   ]
```

### Why growth must be geometric

Copying is O(n), so you might expect appends to be slow. The trick is *how much* to grow.

If capacity **doubles** each time, then, from initial capacity 1, total resizing copies are C − 1, where C is the final capacity. Since n ≤ C < 2n, this is fewer than 2n copies. Spread over n appends, that is fewer than two copies per append: **amortised O(1)**.

Growing by any constant factor `r > 1` works. Ignoring integer rounding, total copying is roughly C / (r − 1), where C is final capacity. At full-capacity endpoints C = n, the following approximations apply; just after growth C is close to rn:

| Growth factor | Copies when n fills final capacity |
|---|---|
| 2 | about n |
| 1.5 | about 2n |
| 1.125 | about 8n |

Growing by a constant *amount* (say +10 slots) does not work. Reaching `n` elements needs n/10 resizes, copying 10 + 20 + 30 + ... elements: O(n²) in total.

> [!warning] Amortised is not worst case
> An individual append that triggers a resize is O(n). If you append to a 10-million-element vector in a latency-sensitive loop, that one append copies 10 million elements. When you know the final size, reserve it up front.

## Real implementations

### Python `list`

A Python list is a dynamic array of **pointers** to objects (8 bytes each on a 64-bit machine), not of the values themselves. `[1, 2, 3]` stores three pointers to three separate `int` objects elsewhere on the heap.

CPython over-allocates by about **12.5%** plus a small constant. The source comments give the capacity sequence as 0, 4, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 52, 64, 76... For a fixed CPython build, sys.getsizeof on an ordinary list can reveal backing-capacity changes. The mild factor saves memory; CPython leans on `realloc`, which can often extend a block in place without copying.

- `append` and `pop()` are amortised O(1).
- `insert(0, x)` and `pop(0)` are O(n). Use `collections.deque` for a queue (lesson 6).
- For dense numbers, `array.array` or NumPy store raw values contiguously, which is far more compact and cache-friendly.

### Java `ArrayList`

`ArrayList` wraps an `Object[]`. A default-constructed list allocates its 10-slot backing array lazily, on the first `add`, and grows by **1.5x** (`old + (old >> 1)`). `ensureCapacity(n)` or `new ArrayList<>(n)` pre-sizes it.

Because Java generics only hold objects, `ArrayList<Integer>` stores references to boxed `Integer` objects. An `int[]` of a million elements is about 4 MB; an `ArrayList<Integer>` of a million is several times that, plus the pointer chasing.

### C++ `std::vector`

`vector` stores elements directly and contiguously. The standard requires amortised constant `push_back` but leaves the growth factor to the implementation: common libraries use factors such as 2 or 1.5 for ordinary incremental growth, but those are implementation details rather than portable guarantees.

`reserve(n)` ensures capacity is at least n without changing size; it does not shrink existing capacity. The crucial pitfall is **invalidation**: a reallocation moves every element, so any pointer, reference or iterator into the vector becomes dangling.

```cpp
std::vector<int> v = {1, 2, 3};
int& first = v[0];
v.push_back(4);  // may reallocate
// 'first' may now dangle: using it is
// undefined behaviour
```

## Shrinking and other pitfalls

- **Shrink thrash.** If you double when full and halve when below half full, a workload that alternates push and pop right at the boundary resizes on every operation. The standard fix is to halve only when the array falls to a **quarter** full. CPython shrinks only when length drops below half the allocated size, and then reallocates with room to spare.
- **Wasted capacity.** After growth, up to half the slots (with doubling) may be empty. C++ shrink_to_fit makes a nonbinding request to reduce capacity; Java trimToSize reduces backing capacity to size. Allocators and garbage collectors determine when memory is reclaimed or returned to the OS.
- **Off-by-one errors.** The last valid index is `len − 1`. In C there is no bounds check, so reading or writing `a[len]` has undefined behavior, which can corrupt memory, crash or behave unpredictably, a classic source of security bugs.

## Key takeaways
- An array is contiguous, same-sized slots, so `a[i]` is one address calculation: O(1).
- Contiguity gives cache-friendly scans; this matters as much as Big-O in practice.
- Inserting or deleting anywhere but the end shifts elements: O(n).
- Dynamic arrays grow geometrically, which makes append amortised O(1); additive growth would be O(n²).
- Python lists hold pointers and grow ~12.5%; ArrayList grows 1.5x; vector grows 2x or 1.5x depending on the library.
- Reallocation invalidates pointers and iterators into a C++ vector.

questions.prompt: An array of 4-byte integers starts at address 2000. At what address does element `a[7]` live?

options.explanation: Correct. address = base + i × size = 2000 + 7 × 4 = 2028.
This adds the index directly, forgetting that each element is 4 bytes wide. That would only be right for a byte array.
This is 2000 + 8 × 4, treating the array as 1-indexed. With 0-based indexing, a[7] is seven elements past the start, not eight.

options.text: It depends on where a[6] was stored
options.explanation: That's how a linked list works. In an array the slots are contiguous, so the address is computed from the base alone; no earlier element needs to be consulted.

questions.workedExample:
1. Formula: `address(i) = base + i * size`.
2. base = 2000, i = 7, size = 4 bytes.
3. 7 × 4 = 28.
4. 2000 + 28 = **2028**.

Check with small cases: a[0] is at 2000 (offset 0), a[1] at 2004, a[2] at 2008. Each step adds 4. That's why indexing is O(1): it is one multiply and one add, regardless of the array's length.

questions.prompt: You have a Python list `nums` of one million **unsorted** integers. What are the costs of `nums[500000]` and `42 in nums` respectively?

options.text: O(1) and O(1)
options.explanation: Indexing is O(1), but membership in a list is not: unlike a set or dict there's no hashing, so Python has to compare against elements one by one.

options.text: O(n) and O(n)
options.explanation: This mistakes indexing for walking the list. A list is an array of pointers, so the slot is found by address arithmetic, not by stepping from the start.

options.text: O(log n) and O(n)
options.explanation: O(log n) is binary search on sorted data. Indexing by position needs no search at all.

options.text: O(1) and O(n)
options.explanation: Correct. Position lookup is base + i × 8 bytes (a pointer slot), O(1). `in` on an unsorted list is a linear scan, O(n) in the worst case.

questions.workedExample:
1. `nums[500000]`: CPython computes the slot address directly from the start of its pointer array. O(1).
2. `42 in nums`: the list has no index on values, so Python compares 42 with nums[0], nums[1], ... until it finds a match or reaches the end. Worst case: one million comparisons. O(n).
3. If you need fast membership tests, convert to a `set` (average O(1) per lookup, covered in the hash tables module). If the data is sorted, `bisect` gives O(log n).

questions.prompt: Which of these Python list operations is O(n) rather than O(1) (amortised)?

options.text: `a.append(x)`
options.explanation: Append writes into spare capacity at the end. It occasionally resizes, but geometric growth makes it amortised O(1).

options.text: `a.insert(0, x)`
options.explanation: Correct. Inserting at the front shifts every existing element one slot to the right, so it costs time proportional to the list's length.

options.text: `a.pop()`
options.explanation: Popping from the end needs no shifting; CPython may occasionally shrink the backing allocation, so the guarantee is amortised.
Negative indexing is just `len(a) - 1`, still one address calculation.

questions.workedExample:
Ask of each operation: does it move other elements? (Each is applied to the original `a`.)

```
a = [A, B, C, D]

append(E):   [A, B, C, D, E]
             nothing moves
pop():       [A, B, C]
             nothing moves
insert(0,X): [X, A, B, C, D]
             A..D all shift
```

The front insert moves all n elements: O(n). If you need cheap inserts and removals at the front, use `collections.deque`.

questions.prompt: A dynamic array starts with capacity 1 and **doubles** whenever an append finds it full. You append 17 elements to an empty array. How many element copies are made by resizing, in total?

options.explanation: That counts only the last resize (copying 16 elements into capacity 32). Earlier resizes also copied elements.
136 is 1 + 2 + ... + 16, which is what you'd get if the array grew by one slot each time. Doubling avoids exactly that quadratic cost.
Correct. Resizes happen when appending the 2nd, 3rd, 5th, 9th and 17th elements, copying 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31 elements.
17 is the number of appends (each writes one element), not the number of copies made by resizing.

questions.workedExample:
Track capacity as you go:

```
append  cap before  resize? copies
  1        1         no      0
  2        1       ->2       1
  3        2       ->4       2
  4        4         no      0
  5        4       ->8       4
  9        8       ->16      8
 17       16       ->32     16
```

Total = 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = **31**, final capacity 32.

This is the amortised argument in action: 31 copies for 17 appends is under 2 per append. In general doubling copies fewer than 2n elements to reach n, so append is amortised O(1).

questions.prompt: Starting empty with capacity 100, a home-grown dynamic array grows by a fixed **100 slots** each time it fills. A job appends 1,000,000 items. Roughly how does the total copying work scale?

options.text: O(n): about one copy per append
options.explanation: That holds for geometric growth. With fixed increments, each resize copies a larger array, and there are n/100 of them.

options.text: O(n log n)
options.explanation: There's no halving or doubling here, so no log factor appears. The copies form an arithmetic series.

options.text: O(1), because each resize only adds 100 slots
options.explanation: Adding the slots is cheap, but the resize must copy every existing element into the new block. That copy is the expensive part.

options.text: O(n²): about 5 billion element copies
options.explanation: Correct. There are 9,999 resizes copying 100, 200, ..., 999,900 elements. That sum is about n²/200 = 5 × 10⁹.

questions.workedExample:
1. Number of resizes after the initial allocation: 1,000,000 / 100 − 1 = 9,999.
2. Resize k copies about 100k elements.
3. Total = 100 × (1 + 2 + ... + 9,999) = 100 × 9,999 × 10,000 / 2 ≈ 5.0 × 10⁹.
4. In general: n/c resizes, total ≈ n² / (2c). Quadratic.
5. Compare doubling: total copies < 2n = 2 × 10⁶. That's about 2,500 times less work.

The fix is to multiply capacity (×1.5 or ×2), not add to it.

options.text: `p` may dangle: reallocation moves the elements, so `*p` is undefined behaviour
options.explanation: Correct. When capacity runs out, vector allocates a new block, moves the elements and frees the old one. Pointers, references and iterators into the old block are invalidated.

options.text: `push_back` is O(n), so the loop is quadratic
options.explanation: `push_back` is amortised O(1). The loop is linear overall; performance isn't the problem.

options.text: Nothing; it prints 1
options.explanation: It might print 1 by luck, but the vector almost certainly reallocated while growing from 3 to 103 elements, so `p` points into freed memory.

options.text: It doesn't compile: you can't take the address of a vector element
options.explanation: Taking `&v[0]` is perfectly legal (it's how you pass vector data to C APIs). The bug is using it after the vector may have moved.

questions.workedExample:
1. `v` starts with size 3 and some small capacity (often 3).
2. `p` points at the first slot of that block.
3. Appending past capacity triggers reallocation: new block (say capacity 6, then 12, 24, ...), elements copied, old block freed.
4. `p` still holds the old address. Dereferencing it reads freed memory: undefined behaviour. It may print 1, garbage, or crash, and sanitizers flag it.
5. Fixes: call `v.reserve(103)` before taking `p`, or store the **index** 0 and use `v[0]` later.

questions.prompt: Which statements about CPython's `list` are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: It stores pointers to objects, not the objects themselves
options.explanation: Correct. Each slot is a pointer (8 bytes on 64-bit). The int or str objects live separately on the heap, which is why lists can hold mixed types.

options.text: It over-allocates so that most appends need no reallocation
options.explanation: Correct. The growth rule adds about 12.5% plus a small constant, giving capacities 4, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 52, ...

options.text: `[1, 2, 3, 4]` stores the four integer values in one contiguous block of 4-byte slots
options.explanation: Incorrect. That describes `array.array('i')` or a NumPy array. A list's contiguous block holds pointers; the int objects themselves are elsewhere.

options.text: `pop(0)` is O(n) because the remaining elements shift left
options.explanation: Correct. Removing the first slot moves every other pointer down by one. Use `collections.deque.popleft()` for O(1).

options.text: It doubles its capacity each time it fills, like libstdc++'s vector
options.explanation: Incorrect. CPython's factor is about 1.125, much milder than doubling. Growth is still geometric, so append is still amortised O(1).

questions.workedExample:
1. Layout: a list object holds a length, a capacity (`allocated`) and a pointer to an array of `PyObject*`.
2. Growth: `new_allocated = (n + (n >> 3) + 6) & ~3`. For n = 9 that's (9 + 1 + 6) & ~3 = 16.
3. You can observe capacity jumps with `sys.getsizeof`, which grows in steps of 8 bytes per extra slot.
4. `pop(0)` shifts n − 1 pointers: O(n).
5. For compact numeric storage use `array` or NumPy, which store raw machine values contiguously.

questions.prompt: In C, `double grid[4096][4096]` (128 MiB with 8-byte doubles) is summed two ways. Loop A iterates `for r ... for c ... grid[r][c]`; loop B swaps the loops: `for c ... for r ... grid[r][c]`. Both do 16.7 million additions. Assuming 64-byte cache lines and no loop interchange, which access pattern is usually more cache-friendly, and why?

options.text: They take the same time; both are O(n²)
options.explanation: Big-O hides constant factors. Here memory access patterns differ wildly, and that dominates real running time.

options.text: B, because columns are stored contiguously in C
options.explanation: That's column-major order, used by Fortran and MATLAB. C is row-major.

options.text: A, because C is row-major: A walks memory sequentially, using every byte of each cache line
options.explanation: Correct. In A, consecutive accesses are 8 bytes apart, so each 64-byte cache line serves 8 doubles and the prefetcher streams ahead. In B, each access jumps 4096 × 8 = 32 KB, touching a new cache line almost every time.

options.text: B, because the compiler always vectorises the inner loop better
options.explanation: Vectorisation favours contiguous inner loops, which helps A, not B. Compilers can sometimes interchange loops, but you shouldn't rely on it.

questions.workedExample:
1. Row-major: `address(r, c) = base + (r * 4096 + c) * 8`.
2. Loop A, inner loop over c: addresses step by 8 bytes. One 64-byte line serves 8 consecutive accesses: eight reads per line when aligned; actual misses and prefetch effectiveness depend on the cache state.
3. Loop B, inner loop over r: addresses step by 4096 × 8 = 32,768 bytes. Each access is a new line. With 4096 rows, the lines from one column are typically evicted before the next column needs them.
4. Result: B can be several times slower, despite identical arithmetic.
5. Rule: make the innermost loop run along the contiguous dimension.

questions.prompt: A dynamic array grows by a factor of **1.5** whenever it is full. Approximately how many element copies does resizing perform, in total, at a full-capacity endpoint of approximately 1,000,000 elements? Ignore integer rounding and initial constant capacity.

options.explanation: That's the figure for doubling (factor 2). A smaller factor means more frequent resizes and more total copying.
Correct. The copies form a geometric series n/r + n/r² + ... = n/(r − 1). With r = 1.5, that's n/0.5 = 2n.
This multiplies n by the growth factor, but the total is governed by 1/(r − 1), not by r itself.

options.text: About 20,000,000 (n log n)
options.explanation: The resize sizes shrink geometrically going backwards, so their sum is bounded by a constant times n. No log factor appears.

questions.workedExample:
1. The last resize copies about n/1.5 elements, the one before about n/1.5², and so on.
2. Total ≈ n × (1/r + 1/r² + 1/r³ + ...) = n × (1/r) / (1 − 1/r) = n / (r − 1).
3. r = 1.5: n / 0.5 = 2n ≈ **2,000,000** copies.
4. Compare: r = 2 gives about n; CPython's r ≈ 1.125 gives about 8n.
For an arbitrary stopping length, replace n by final capacity C in the series; C can approach rn. Thus the copies can approach 3n for r = 1.5.
5. All are O(n) total, so append is amortised O(1) in every case. The trade-off is copying versus wasted space: r = 2 can leave up to half the capacity empty; r = 1.5 at most a third.

questions.prompt: A stack backed by a dynamic array doubles capacity when a push finds it full, and **halves** capacity whenever a pop leaves length at half of capacity or less. It holds exactly 1,024 elements at capacity 1,024. A workload now alternates `push, pop, push, pop, ...` forever. What happens?

options.text: Each push doubles to 2,048 and each pop halves back to 1,024, so every operation copies about 1,000 elements
options.explanation: Correct. This is resize thrashing. The push at 1,024/1,024 grows to 2,048 (copying 1,024); the pop leaves 1,024/2,048, exactly half, so it shrinks back (copying 1,024). Every operation pays O(n). Shrinking only at one-quarter full prevents it.

options.text: Every operation stays O(1) amortised
options.explanation: The amortised guarantee breaks here: the policy lets a single cheap operation undo the resize just paid for.

options.text: The array grows without bound
options.explanation: The pops balance the pushes, so length oscillates around 1,024; capacity bounces rather than grows.

options.text: Nothing; the shrink never triggers because length never falls below 1,024
options.explanation: The rule fires at half *or less*, and after the push grows capacity to 2,048, a pop back to 1,024 is exactly half.

questions.workedExample:
Trace from length 1,024, capacity 1,024:

```
op    len   cap   resize
push  1025  2048  grow, copy 1024
pop   1024  1024  shrink, copy 1024
push  1025  2048  grow, copy 1024
pop   1024  1024  shrink, copy 1024
```

Every single operation copies about 1,000 elements, so the 'amortised O(1)' stack is now O(n) per operation.

Fix: **shrink to half only when length falls to a quarter of capacity**. After growing to 2,048, you'd need to pop down to 512 before shrinking, so at least ~n/2 cheap operations separate any two resizes. That restores amortised O(1). (Even a strict 'below half' rule is fragile: a push, pop, pop, push, push pattern still thrashes.)

questions.prompt: A Java service stores 10 million independently boxed sensor readings outside the Integer cache range in an `ArrayList<Integer>`. Which statements about switching to `int[]` are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Memory drops substantially, because each element becomes a 4-byte value instead of a reference to a separate boxed `Integer` object
options.explanation: Correct. An `Integer` object costs roughly 16 bytes plus a 4–8 byte reference in the list, against 4 bytes in an `int[]`. Expect several-fold savings.

options.text: Summing needs fewer indirections and gains contiguous primitive storage, which can improve speed
options.explanation: Correct. An `int[]` streams through the cache. `ArrayList<Integer>` stores references that point to objects scattered on the heap, so each read is an extra indirection and a possible cache miss.

options.text: Appending becomes cheaper, because `int[]` grows by 2x instead of 1.5x
options.explanation: Incorrect. `int[]` is a static array: it can't grow at all. You'd have to manage resizing yourself (or pre-size it).

options.text: Pre-sizing with `new ArrayList<>(10_000_000)` would avoid both the boxing and the pointer chasing
options.explanation: Incorrect. Pre-sizing avoids the resize copies, but the list still holds references to boxed `Integer` objects.

options.text: Garbage-collection work falls, since there are far fewer objects for the collector to track
options.explanation: Correct. One `int[]` is a single object. Ten million `Integer`s (outside the small cached range) are ten million extra objects occupying heap space and requiring eventual reclamation.

questions.workedExample:
1. `ArrayList<Integer>` = an `Object[]` of references + one `Integer` object per value (header + 4-byte int, padded to ~16 bytes on a typical 64-bit JVM).
2. Rough size: 10M × (4-byte compressed reference + 16-byte object) ≈ 200 MB, versus 10M × 4 bytes = 40 MB for `int[]`.
3. Access: list read = load reference, then load object (scattered). Array read = one sequential load.
4. `int[]` is fixed-size; growth is your problem (`Arrays.copyOf`).
5. Libraries like fastutil or Eclipse Collections provide resizable primitive lists (`IntArrayList`) that give you both.

lessons.title: Strings
lessons.summary: Strings as arrays of characters, why most languages make them immutable, what encodings do to length and indexing, why concatenating in a loop is quadratic, and the real cost of common string operations.
lessons.body:
A string represents a sequence of text units. Many implementations use arrays, but indexing cost depends on which units are requested and how the string is represented. But strings come with two complications that trip up beginners and experienced engineers alike:

1. In most modern languages they are **immutable**: you can never change one, only make a new one.
2. A "character" is not as simple as it sounds. How many bytes it takes depends on the **encoding**.

Both have real performance and correctness consequences.

## Immutability

In Python, Java, JavaScript, C# and Go, a string object can never be modified after it is created.

```python
s = "hello"
s[0] = "H"      # TypeError: 'str' object
                # does not support item
                # assignment
s = "H" + s[1:] # builds a new string
```

Operations that look like modification (`upper()`, `replace()`, `+`) return an immutable string value and leave the original contents alone; an implementation may reuse an existing object when the result is unchanged. A variable can be re-pointed at a new string, but any other variable still pointing at the old one sees no change.

```python
s = "hello"
t = s
s += " world"
print(t)        # hello
```

C++ std::string and Rust String are mutable growable buffers with separate borrowed-view types, std::string_view and &str. C char arrays can be mutable but C does not provide those ownership/view types.

### Why make strings immutable?

- **Safe as hash keys.** A dict or HashMap stores a key in a bucket chosen by its hash. If the key could change, it would sit in the wrong bucket forever. Immutable strings can also **cache** their hash: Python and Java compute it once and store it.
- **Free sharing.** Many variables, threads or data structures can point at the same string with no copying and no locks, because nobody can change it.
- **Interning.** Identical literals can share one object. Java interns string literals; CPython interns many identifiers and short strings.
- **Security.** A checked string value cannot change through an alias. This does not prevent the file, permissions or other external resource named by it from changing between check and use.

Changing the text generally requires producing another value; allocation and copying may be optimized when observable immutability is preserved.

## Encoding basics

Computers store bytes, not letters. An **encoding** maps characters to bytes.

- **ASCII** covers 128 characters (English letters, digits, punctuation) in 7 bits.
- **Unicode** assigns a number, a **code point**, to over 150,000 characters: `U+0041` is `A`, `U+00E9` is `é`, `U+1F600` is 😀.
- **UTF-8** stores each Unicode scalar value in 1 to 4 bytes; surrogate code points are excluded. ASCII characters take 1 byte, so plain ASCII text is valid UTF-8. It is the dominant encoding on the web and in files.
- **UTF-16** uses 2 bytes for most common characters and 4 bytes (a **surrogate pair**) for the rest, including most emoji.

```
char   code point  UTF-8 bytes  UTF-16 units
A      U+0041      1            1
é      U+00E9      2            1
€      U+20AC      3            1
😀     U+1F600     4            2
```

### What does "length" mean?

Different languages count different things:

```python
s = "café"
len(s)                  # 4 code points
len(s.encode("utf-8"))  # 5 bytes
len("😀")               # 1
```

In Java and JavaScript, `"😀".length()` / `"😀".length` is **2**, because they count UTF-16 code units. Slicing such a string in the wrong place splits a surrogate pair and produces garbage.

Even code points aren't what a reader thinks of as a character. `é` can be one code point (`U+00E9`) or two (`e` plus a combining accent `U+0301`). The two forms look identical but compare unequal unless you **normalise** them (Python's `unicodedata.normalize`). A flag emoji like 🇬🇧 is two code points. What users perceive as one character is a **grapheme cluster**.

### How runtimes store strings

- **CPython** (PEP 393) picks 1, 2 or 4 bytes per code point for each string, based on the widest character it contains. Every code point then has a fixed width, so `s[i]` stays O(1). One emoji in a long ASCII string makes the whole string 4 bytes per character.
- **Java 9+** uses "compact strings": Latin-1 (1 byte per char) when possible, otherwise UTF-16.
- **Rust String** stores valid UTF-8. **Go strings** are arbitrary byte sequences, conventionally UTF-8 for text. Getting the *i*-th code point means scanning from the start, O(n), which is why Rust doesn't let you write `s[i]` on a `String` and Go's `s[i]` gives you a byte.

## Concatenation cost

Because strings are immutable, `a + b` allocates a new string of length `len(a) + len(b)` and copies both in. That is O(len(a) + len(b)).

Now put it in a loop:

```python
result = ""
for word in words:   # n words
    result += word   # copies all of result
```

If each word has length k, iteration i copies about i·k characters. Total: k + 2k + ... + nk ≈ **k·n²/2**. That's quadratic. For 100,000 one-character pieces, about 5 billion character copies.

> [!note] CPython sometimes cheats
> CPython can extend `result` in place when nothing else references it, which often makes this loop fast in practice. It's an implementation detail: it disappears if another reference exists, and PEP 8 says not to rely on it. It is not a portable guarantee across Python implementations.

### The fix: collect, then join

Gather the pieces in a list (amortised O(1) appends), then join once. `join` measures the total length, allocates once, and copies each piece once: **O(number of pieces + total length)**.

```python
parts = []
for word in words:
    parts.append(word)
result = "".join(parts)
```

In Java, use `StringBuilder`, a mutable, growable character buffer (a dynamic array, so appending k units costs amortised O(k + 1)):

```java
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (String w : words) {
    sb.append(w);
}
String result = sb.toString();
```

> [!warning] The compiler won't save you in a loop
> `javac` turns a single expression like `a + b + c` into one efficient concatenation. But `s = s + w` inside a loop still builds a brand-new string on every iteration. The loop remains O(n²).

## Common operations and their complexity

For a string of length n (Python and Java, which store their length and support O(1) indexing):

| Operation | Cost | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `len(s)` | O(1) | Length is stored |
| `s[i]` | O(1) | Fixed-width units |
| `s[a:b]` | O(b − a) | Copies a new string |
| `a == b` | O(n) | Stops at first difference |
| `t in s` | O(n·m) worst | Usually much faster |
| `upper` | O(n) | Unicode case conversion |
| literal `split`, `replace` | Depends on search and output size | Replacement can expand the output |
| `"".join(parts)` | O(pieces + output length) | Must inspect empty pieces too |

A few details matter here:

- **C's `strlen` is O(n).** C strings are byte arrays ending in a zero byte, and the length is found by scanning for it. Writing `for (i = 0; i < strlen(s); i++)` makes the loop O(n²) unless the compiler hoists the call.
- **Slices copy.** In Python, `s[1:]` is a new string. Recursive functions that pass `s[1:]` down at each level copy O(n) per call: O(n²) total. Pass indices instead. Java's `substring` has also copied since Java 7u6; earlier versions shared the parent's array, which caused memory leaks when a tiny substring kept a huge string alive.
- **Substring search.** A naive search tries every start position, O(n·m) in the worst case. Library implementations use cleverer algorithms and are fast on typical text; CPython adopted the linear-time two-way algorithm for longer needles in Python 3.10. Linear-time algorithms such as KMP appear in a later module.
- **Hashing** is O(n) the first time, but Python and Java cache the result on the string object.

## Pitfalls in practice

- **Byte limits vs character limits.** A database column, HTTP header or SMS segment limited in bytes can overflow on text that looks short. Truncating UTF-8 at a byte boundary can slice a character in half and produce invalid data. Truncate on code points (or graphemes), then check the byte length.
- **Identity vs equality.** In Python, `a is b` asks "same object?", not "same text?". Interning makes it accidentally true for some literals and false for strings built at runtime. In Java, `==` on `String` compares references; use `.equals()`.
- **Repeated `replace` or `+` in hot paths.** Each creates a new string. Build once with a builder or `join`.
- **Reversing user-visible text.** `s[::-1]` reverses code points, which mangles combining accents and multi-code-point emoji.

## Key takeaways
- A string is an array of code units: O(1) indexing and length in Python and Java; O(n) `strlen` in C.
- Immutability makes strings safe to share and to use as hash keys, at the cost of copying on every change.
- UTF-8 uses 1–4 bytes per Unicode scalar value; Java and JavaScript lengths count UTF-16 units, so an emoji has length 2.
- `s += piece` in a loop is O(n²) in general. Use `"".join(list)` or `StringBuilder` for O(n).
- Slicing copies, so passing `s[1:]` down a recursion is quadratic; pass indices.

options.text: Strings are immutable, so their hash can never change after the key is stored
options.explanation: Correct. A dict places each key in a slot chosen by its hash. A mutable key could change, its hash would no longer match its slot, and lookups would fail. Strings can even cache their hash.

options.explanation: Python lists are dynamic arrays, and anything can in principle be hashed. The issue is that a list's contents, and so its hash, could change while it's a key.

1. `d["apple"] = 1` computes `hash("apple")` and stores the entry in the slot that hash points to.
2. Later, `d["apple"]` hashes again and looks in the same slot. This works only if the hash is stable.

questions.prompt: Which are genuine benefits of making strings immutable, as Java and Python do? Select all that apply.

options.text: A string's hash code can be computed once and cached, making repeated map lookups cheaper
options.explanation: Correct. Java's `String.hashCode()` and CPython's str hash are cached on the object because the contents can never change.

options.text: Strings can be shared between threads without locks
options.explanation: Correct. No thread can modify a shared string, so there are no data races on its contents.

options.text: Concatenation in a loop becomes O(n)
options.explanation: Incorrect. Immutability is exactly why naive concatenation is O(n²): a flat-buffer implementation without in-place optimization recopies the growing prefix.

options.text: Identical strings can be interned so that many references share one object
options.explanation: Correct. Interning is only safe because nobody can change the shared object out from under the other users.

options.text: It allows O(1) indexing in UTF-8
options.explanation: Incorrect. Immutability says nothing about encoding. O(1) indexing comes from fixed-width storage (Latin-1, UTF-16 units, PEP 393), not from immutability; UTF-8 indexing by code point is O(n) either way.

questions.workedExample:
Think about what each benefit requires:

1. **Hash caching** requires that the contents never change after the first `hashCode()` call. Immutability guarantees that.
2. **Lock-free sharing** requires no writers. Immutability means there are none.
3. **Interning** requires that changing one 'copy' can't affect another. With immutability there's no changing.
4. **Concatenation** is the price you pay: edits generally produce new values, with allocation depending on implementation. Use builders.
5. **Indexing speed** is a storage-layout question. A mutable UTF-8 string would still need an O(n) scan to find code point i.

questions.prompt: Before Java 7u6, `String.substring` returned a view sharing the parent's `char[]`. A service read 50-million-byte ASCII log files into Strings, kept a 20-character `substring` of each as an ID in a long-lived cache, and discarded the rest. What happened?

options.text: Each cached ID kept its whole 50 MB backing array alive, causing a memory leak
options.explanation: Correct. The GC can't free the parent array while any substring still references it. This is why Java 7u6 changed `substring` to copy: O(k) time but no hidden retention.

options.text: Memory use stayed small, since each ID was only 20 characters
options.explanation: That's the post-7u6 behaviour, where substring copies. With sharing, each tiny ID kept a reference to the entire 50 MB array.

options.text: The IDs became corrupted when the original Strings were garbage-collected
options.explanation: The GC never frees memory that's still reachable. The shared array stayed alive precisely because the substrings referenced it, so nothing was corrupted.

options.text: `substring` threw an exception for strings over 2 GB
options.explanation: The files were 50 MB each, well within array limits. The problem was retention, not size.

questions.workedExample:
1. Old design: `String` held `(char[] value, int offset, int count)`. `substring` made a new String with the same `value` and a different offset/count: O(1) time, no copying.
2. Downside: the 20-character ID still references the 50-million-char backing array (about 100 MB, since Java chars were 2 bytes).
3. 1,000 cached IDs → up to ~100 GB of arrays that can't be collected.
4. Workaround then: `new String(s.substring(a, b))` forced a copy.
5. Since 7u6, `substring` copies the k characters. Ordinary proper CPython str slices copy; empty or whole-string slices can reuse existing objects. The trade-off: sharing makes slicing O(1) but risks retention; copying makes it O(k) but predictable.

lessons.title: Linked lists
lessons.summary: Singly, doubly and circular linked lists, how sentinel nodes remove edge cases, the real costs of insertion and deletion, and the specific situations where linked lists beat arrays.
lessons.body:
An array keeps its elements side by side. A **linked list** gives that up: each element lives in its own **node**, anywhere in memory, and each node holds a pointer to the next one.

```
head
 |
 v
[3|*]--->[8|*]--->[5|*]--->None
 val next
```

That one change flips the trade-offs:

- You can no longer jump to element `i`; you must walk there. Access becomes **O(n)**.
- But if you already hold a node, you can insert or remove next to it by rewiring a couple of pointers, with no shifting. That's **O(1)**.

Linked lists are a staple of interviews and textbooks. In production code they are less common than you might expect, and knowing *why* is part of mastering them.

## Singly linked lists

Each node has a value and a `next` pointer. The list itself is just a reference to the first node, the **head**. The last node's `next` is `None`.

```python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next

# build 3 -> 8 -> 5
head = Node(3, Node(8, Node(5)))
```

### Traversal and search

```python
def find(head, target):
    cur = head
    while cur:
        if cur.val == target:
            return cur
        cur = cur.next
    return None
```

Getting the k-th element, or searching for a value, is O(n): you follow k pointers.

### Insertion

Inserting at the head is O(1), and so is inserting after a node you already hold:

```python
# push to front
head = Node(1, head)

# insert x after node p
p.next = Node(x, p.next)
```

```
before:  p -> [8] -> [5]
after:   p -> [x] -> [8] -> [5]
```

Order matters. Create the new node pointing at `p.next` *first*, then point `p` at it. Do it the other way round and you lose the rest of the list.

Inserting at the tail is O(n) unless you also keep a `tail` pointer, in which case it is O(1).

### Deletion

To remove a node you need the node **before** it, so you can skip over it:

```python
# remove the node after p
p.next = p.next.next
```

This is the singly linked list's big weakness. Given only a pointer to a node, you can't unlink it in O(1), because you can't reach its predecessor without walking from the head. Removing the head is a special case (`head = head.next`), and that special-casing is a common source of bugs.

## Doubly linked lists

Add a `prev` pointer to every node and you can walk in both directions, and delete any node in O(1) given only that node:

```
None<-[3]<=>[8]<=>[5]->None
```

```python
def unlink(node):
    node.prev.next = node.next
    node.next.prev = node.prev
```

That code crashes when `node` is the head (`node.prev` is `None`) or the tail. Handling those cases with `if` statements everywhere is tedious and error-prone. Which brings us to sentinels.

## Sentinel nodes

A **sentinel** (or dummy) node is a node that holds no data and is always present. With a sentinel, the list is never truly empty and every real node always has a real neighbour on both sides.

The neatest version is a **circular doubly linked list with one sentinel**: the sentinel's `next` is the first element and its `prev` is the last.

```
   +--------------------------+
   v                          |
[sent] <=> [3] <=> [8] <=> [5]
   |                          ^
   +--------------------------+

empty list: sent.next = sent.prev = sent
```

```python
class DNode:
    def __init__(self, val=None):
        self.val = val
        self.prev = self.next = self

class DList:
    def __init__(self):
        self.s = DNode()   # sentinel

    def insert_after(self, p, val):
        n = DNode(val)
        n.prev, n.next = p, p.next
        p.next.prev = n
        p.next = n
        return n

    def push_front(self, val):
        s = self.s
        return self.insert_after(s, val)

    def push_back(self, val):
        last = self.s.prev
        return self.insert_after(last, val)

    def remove(self, n):
        n.prev.next = n.next
        n.next.prev = n.prev
```

For valid handles belonging to this list, insertion and removal use a constant number of pointer updates. Do not remove the sentinel or remove a node twice. Allocation and value destruction are outside this pointer-operation model. There is no special case for an empty list, the first node or the last node. The Linux kernel's `struct list_head` uses exactly this design, with intrusive link fields embedded in containing objects.

> [!tip] The cost of a sentinel
> One extra node of memory per list. For a list with millions of entries that's nothing; for millions of tiny lists it can add up.

## Circular lists

In a **circular** list the last node points back to the first instead of to `None`. Circular singly linked lists are handy for round-robin scheduling: keep a pointer to the current node and advance it forever.

A neat trick: keep only a **tail** pointer. Then `tail.next` is the head, so you get O(1) access to both ends from one pointer.

The danger with circular lists is the loop condition. `while cur:` never ends; you must stop when you return to your starting node.

## Cost summary

| Operation | Array | Singly | Doubly |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access i-th | O(1) | O(n) | O(n) |
| Insert/delete at front | O(n) | O(1) | O(1) |
| Insert/delete at back | O(1) amortised | See below | O(1) |
| Delete given node | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) |
| Insert after given node | O(n) | O(1) | O(1) |

For a singly linked list, inserting at the back is O(1) if you keep a tail pointer, but deleting the last node is O(n), because you have to walk to its predecessor.

## The hidden costs

Big-O makes linked lists look great for insertion-heavy work. Real hardware is less kind.

- **Memory overhead.** Every node carries one or two pointers plus allocator bookkeeping. A Java `LinkedList` node is an object with three references (item, next, prev); for small elements, the overhead dwarfs the data. A Python node object costs tens of bytes before you even count the value.
- **Cache misses.** Nodes are scattered around the heap. Walking a list is a chain of dependent loads: the CPU can't fetch node 5 until node 4 tells it where node 5 is. Arrays stream through cache with prefetching.
- **Allocation.** Separately allocated nodes add allocation/reclamation work; pools and intrusive lists can avoid a per-insertion allocation.
- **Finding the spot is O(n) anyway.** "Insert in the middle is O(1)" assumes you already hold the node. If you have to search for the position first, that search is O(n), and on an array it is a fast linear scan.

> [!example] Why locality can outweigh shifting
> A vector can beat a linked list when both first perform a linear search for the insertion point: contiguous scanning and shifting may outweigh the cost of moving elements. Actual performance requires measurement.

> [!note] Evidence gap
> A specific historical benchmark result is omitted because its exact dataset, implementation and measurements have not been independently reproduced or sourced here.

## When linked lists actually win

Linked lists earn their place when you **already hold a reference** to the node you want to change, or when you need properties arrays can't give:

1. **O(1) removal from the middle via a handle.** An LRU cache pairs a hash map (key to node) with a doubly linked list. On every hit it unlinks the node and moves it to the front in O(1). This is how Python's `OrderedDict` and Java's `LinkedHashMap` keep order.
2. **Stable references.** Inserting into or removing from a `std::list` never invalidates iterators to other elements. A vector's reallocation invalidates all of them.
3. **Splicing.** Relinking a run with known boundaries takes a few pointer changes, but maintaining container metadata can add work. C++ std::list range-splice between different lists is linear in the range length; whole-list and single-element splice are constant-time under their allocator preconditions.
4. **No reallocation spikes.** A linked queue never has to copy everything to grow, but allocation, reclamation and synchronization still need bounded-latency designs for hard real-time use.
5. **Intrusive lists.** In kernels and game engines, the `next`/`prev` pointers live inside the object itself, so membership needs no separate node allocation; simultaneous membership in several lists requires a separate link pair for each list.
6. **Immutable sharing.** In functional languages (Haskell, Lisp, Scala's `List`), prepending to a list creates one new node that points at the old list. Both versions remain valid and share the tail.

Many practical structures are hybrids. CPython's `collections.deque` is a doubly linked list of **blocks**, each holding 64 items. It keeps O(1) operations at both ends while getting most of an array's cache-friendliness.

## Key takeaways
- A linked list trades O(1) indexing for O(1) insertion and deletion next to a node you already hold.
- Singly linked lists can't delete a node without its predecessor; doubly linked lists can, in O(1).
- A sentinel node removes the empty, head and tail special cases; a circular list with one sentinel is the cleanest design.
- Pointer overhead, allocation and cache misses mean arrays usually win in practice, even for insertion-heavy work.
- Use linked lists when you hold node handles (LRU caches), need stable references, splice, or share immutable tails.

options.explanation: Correct. Each node only knows where the next one is, so you walk from the head one step at a time.

options.text: O(1), like an array

options.text: O(log n), using binary search

options.text: O(n) always, even for k = 0

2. `cur = cur.next` takes you to node 1, then node 2, and so on.
3. To reach node k you perform k hops.

```python

for _ in range(k):

return cur.val
```

```python
p = head.next
p.next = Node(9, p.next)
```

What goes wrong if you insert `n` after node `p` in a singly linked list like this?

```python
p.next = n
n.next = p.next
```

options.text: Nothing; the order of the two assignments doesn't matter
options.explanation: It does matter: after the first line, `p.next` is already `n`, so the second line reads the new value, not the old one.

options.text: `n` points to itself, and the rest of the list after `p` is lost
options.explanation: Correct. Line 1 overwrites the only reference to p's old successor. Line 2 then sets `n.next = p.next`, which is `n` itself: a self-loop.

options.text: It raises an AttributeError
options.explanation: Every name involved is a valid node, so no error is raised. The bug is silent, which makes it worse.

options.text: It inserts `n` before `p` instead
options.explanation: Nothing points at `n` from p's predecessor, so it isn't before `p`. It's after `p`, but pointing at itself.

questions.workedExample:
Start: `p -> A -> B`.

1. `p.next = n` → `p -> n`. Nobody references A any more.
2. `n.next = p.next` → `p.next` is now `n`, so `n.next = n`.

```
p -> n --+
     ^   |
     +---+   A -> B lost
```

Any traversal now loops forever at `n`. Correct order: link the new node to the successor first, then link the predecessor to the new node:

```python
n.next = p.next
p.next = n
```

options.text: C, A

options.text: C only, then an error
options.explanation: B's pointers were never cleared, so following `C.prev` reaches B and then A without error.

options.text: C, B, A
options.explanation: Correct. Forward links skip B, but `C.prev` still points to B, and `B.prev` still points to A. The list is now inconsistent in the two directions.

options.text: An infinite loop
options.explanation: No pointer was made to form a cycle. Backward links still form the original chain C → B → A → None.

questions.workedExample:
1. Before: A.next = B, B.next = C; C.prev = B, B.prev = A.
2. Buggy remove sets only `A.next = C`.
3. Forward: A → C. Looks right.
4. Backward: C.prev = **B** (unchanged) → B.prev = A → None. Output: C, B, A.

```python
node.prev.next = node.next
node.next.prev = node.prev
```

questions.prompt: You implement a doubly linked list as a **circular list with a single sentinel node**. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: An empty list is a sentinel whose `next` and `prev` both point to itself
options.explanation: Correct. That's the base state, and it means `s.next` and `s.prev` are never `None`.

options.text: `remove(node)` needs no special cases for the first or last element
options.explanation: Correct. Every real node has real neighbours on both sides (possibly the sentinel), so the same two pointer updates always work.

options.text: `push_back` is O(n) because you must walk to the end
options.explanation: Incorrect. The last element is `s.prev`, available in O(1), so `push_back` is O(1).

options.text: The list is empty exactly when `s.next is s`
options.explanation: Correct. That's how the Linux kernel's `list_empty` works: the head's `next` points back at the head.

options.text: Traversal can stop when `cur is None`
options.explanation: Incorrect. Nothing is ever `None` in a circular list, so that loop never terminates. Stop when you arrive back at the sentinel.

1. Empty: `s.next = s.prev = s`.
2. push_back(5): insert after `s.prev` (which is `s`). Now `s <-> 5 <-> s`.
3. remove(5): `5.prev.next = 5.next` → `s.next = s`; `5.next.prev = 5.prev` → `s.prev = s`. Back to empty with no `if`s.

```python
cur = s.next
while cur is not s:

```

options.text: LinkedList is synchronised, so every call takes a lock

questions.workedExample:
1. `LinkedList.get(i)` starts from the head if i < n/2, otherwise from the tail.
2. Cost of get(i) = min(i, n − 1 − i). Averaged over i, that's about n/4 hops.
3. n calls × n/4 hops = n²/4 = (10⁵)²/4 = 2.5 × 10⁹ hops, with dependent loads whose cache-hit rate depends on allocation and working set.
4. Fix A: `for (Order o : orders) process(o);` → one pass, n hops.
5. Fix B: use `ArrayList`, where `get(i)` is O(1).

questions.prompt: In which scenario does a doubly linked list clearly beat a dynamic array?

options.text: An LRU cache that, on each hit, must move an entry (found via a hash map) to the front
options.explanation: Correct. The hash map hands you the node directly, so unlinking it and re-inserting at the front is O(1). An array would have to shift up to n elements.

options.text: Reading elements by index for a paginated API
options.explanation: Index access is O(1) for an array and O(n) for a list. This is an array's best case.

options.text: Storing 10 million floats and repeatedly summing them
options.explanation: Summing is a sequential scan, where an array's contiguous layout and prefetching win easily. The list adds two pointers per float and a cache miss per node.

options.text: Appending log lines to the end and occasionally reading the last 100
options.explanation: Append is amortised O(1) on an array and the last 100 are contiguous. A list offers no advantage and costs more memory.

questions.workedExample:
Ask: do I already have a reference to the node I need to modify, and must I modify the middle?

1. LRU hit on key K: `node = map[K]` (O(1)).
2. Unlink: `node.prev.next = node.next; node.next.prev = node.prev` (O(1)).
3. Insert after the sentinel (O(1)).
4. Array alternative: find K's position (O(1) via map), but moving it to the front shifts everything before it (O(n)), and stored positions of the shifted entries must be updated.

In the other scenarios you either scan or index, where arrays win.

questions.prompt: You insert integers one at a time into a sorted sequence, using a linear search then insertion. Why can std::vector outperform std::list despite shifting elements? This asks about an architectural possibility, not a measured benchmark.

options.text: The list was much faster, because its insert is O(1) while the vector's is O(n)
options.explanation: Both are O(n) per operation, because the list still has to do an O(n) linear search to find the insertion point. And the list's search is slow.

options.text: They performed about the same, since both are O(n²) overall
options.explanation: Same complexity, but the constant factors differ by a large margin.

options.text: The vector can benefit from contiguous scanning and shifting, while separately allocated list nodes add dependent pointer loads
options.explanation: Correct. The vector's shift is essentially a `memmove` of contiguous memory, and its scan is cache- and prefetcher-friendly. The list's scan is a chain of dependent loads with frequent cache misses, which can dominate. Actual results depend on the workload and machine.

options.text: The vector was faster only because it used binary search
options.explanation: The question specifies linear search for both. Binary search can also use linked iterators, but finding midpoints still requires linear total traversal rather than random access.

questions.workedExample:
1. Per insert, both structures do: find position (O(n) scan) + insert.
2. Vector insert: shift ~n/2 elements with `memmove`, whose throughput depends on the machine and element type.
3. List insert: allocate a node, rewire 4 pointers. Cheap in itself.
4. But the search: the vector scans contiguous ints (16 per 64-byte cache line, prefetched). The list visits a separate heap node per step; each `next` must load before the following address is known, so the CPU stalls on memory.
5. Possible result: contiguous access outweighs shifting. No specific speedup or historical dataset is asserted here. The lesson: Big-O counts operations, not cache misses.

questions.prompt: A circular **singly** linked list is stored with only a `tail` pointer (so `tail.next` is the head). Which operations are O(1)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Insert at the front
options.explanation: Correct. Create `n`, set `n.next = tail.next`, then `tail.next = n`. The tail doesn't change.

options.text: Insert at the back
options.explanation: Correct. Insert at the front as above, then advance `tail = n`. The new node becomes the tail.

options.text: Remove from the front
options.explanation: Correct. `tail.next = tail.next.next` skips the old head (handle the one-element case by setting tail to None).

options.text: Remove from the back
options.explanation: Incorrect. You'd need the node before the tail to make it the new tail, and in a singly linked list that means walking all the way round: O(n).

options.text: Read the k-th element
options.explanation: Incorrect. Still O(k): circularity doesn't give random access.

questions.workedExample:
List 1 → 2 → 3 → (back to 1), tail = 3.

```
push_front(0):
  n.next = tail.next  (0 -> 1)
  tail.next = n       (3 -> 0)
  0 1 2 3, tail 3

push_back(4):
  push_front(4), then tail = 4
  0 1 2 3 4, tail 4

pop_front:
  tail.next = tail.next.next
  1 2 3 4

pop_back: need node 3 to become
  tail, but no prev pointer: walk
  the ring. O(n)
```

That makes this layout a natural O(1) **queue** (push back, pop front) using a single pointer.

questions.prompt: An interview asks you to delete a node from a singly linked list given **only a reference to that node** (not the head). The usual trick is `node.val = node.next.val; node.next = node.next.next`. What is the most serious problem with this in real code?

options.text: It's O(n)
options.explanation: It's O(1): one copy and one pointer change. Complexity isn't the issue.

options.text: It can't delete the last node, and it actually destroys the *next* node's identity, breaking any outside reference to either node
options.explanation: Correct. There's no successor to copy from when deleting the tail. And any code holding a reference to the old successor now holds a node that's no longer in the list, while references to `node` now see a different value.

options.text: It leaks memory in Python because the removed node is never freed
options.explanation: Once nothing references the old successor, Python's reference counting frees it. Leaking isn't the concern.

options.text: It reverses the order of the remaining nodes
options.explanation: Order is preserved: the value from the next node moves back one place, and the list reads correctly afterwards.

questions.workedExample:
List: `A(1) -> B(2) -> C(3) -> D(4)`, and you're given B.

1. `B.val = C.val` → B now holds 3.
2. `B.next = C.next` → `A -> B(3) -> D`.
3. Reads correctly as 1, 3, 4. Node C is detached from the list; external references may keep it alive.
4. Problems:
   - If an LRU map held a reference to C for key 3, it now points to a detached node.
   - Anyone holding B expecting value 2 now sees 3.
   - If given D (the tail), there's no `D.next` to copy: the trick fails.
5. In production, use a doubly linked list if you need O(1) delete-by-handle.

questions.prompt: In Haskell, `xs = [2, 3, 4]` and `ys = 1 : xs` (prepend 1). What does creating `ys` cost, and what happens to `xs`?

options.text: O(1): one new node is created that points at `xs`; both lists stay valid and share the nodes 2, 3, 4
options.explanation: Correct. This is structural sharing. Because no one can mutate the shared nodes, both versions remain correct forever. It's why singly linked lists are the default sequence in functional languages.

options.text: O(n): `xs` is copied into a new list, so `xs` and `ys` are independent
options.explanation: Copying isn't needed. Since lists are immutable, `ys` can safely reuse `xs`'s nodes.

options.text: O(1), but `xs` is now invalid because its head moved
options.explanation: `xs` still points at the node holding 2, which hasn't changed. Nothing about `xs` is altered.

options.text: O(n), because the new head must be linked from the old tail
options.explanation: That describes appending, not prepending. Appending to an immutable list is O(n), because every node on the path must be copied.

questions.workedExample:
```
ys -> [1] -+
           v
xs ------> [2] -> [3] -> [4]
```

1. `1 : xs` allocates one cons cell with value 1 and `next = xs`. O(1).
2. `xs` is untouched; it's still the list starting at 2.
3. Sharing is safe only because the nodes are immutable. In a mutable language, changing `xs[0]` would silently change `ys[1]`.
4. The flip side: appending to the end (`xs ++ [5]`) must copy all n nodes, O(n), since the last node's `next` can't be changed.

lessons.title: Classic linked-list techniques
lessons.summary: The handful of pointer patterns behind almost every linked-list problem — in-place reversal, fast and slow pointers (Floyd's cycle detection, finding the middle), merging sorted lists and dummy heads — with traces and proofs.
lessons.body:
Most linked-list problems, in interviews and in real code, reduce to a few patterns. Learn these four and you can assemble the rest:

1. **Reversal**: turn every arrow around in one pass.
2. **Fast and slow pointers**: two pointers moving at different speeds.
3. **Merging**: weave two sorted lists together.
4. **Dummy heads**: a throwaway node in front so the real head is never a special case.

The iterative patterns below use linear time and **O(1) extra space**; recursive reversal is an explicit exception. Unless detecting a cycle, assume finite acyclic lists. That last part is the point: anyone can solve these problems by copying the list into an array first, but then you've spent O(n) memory.

Throughout, we use:

```python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next
```

## Reversal

Reversing a singly linked list in place means making every `next` point backwards. You need three pointers: the node you're working on (`cur`), the part already reversed (`prev`), and the rest of the list (`nxt`), which you must save before you break the link to it.

```python
def reverse(head):
    prev, cur = None, head
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next   # save the rest
        cur.next = prev  # flip the arrow
        prev = cur       # grow reversed
        cur = nxt        # move on
    return prev          # new head
```

Trace on `1 -> 2 -> 3`:

```
start   prev=None  cur=1   1->2->3
iter 1  None<-1    prev=1  cur=2
iter 2  None<-1<-2 prev=2  cur=3
iter 3  None<-1<-2<-3
        prev=3     cur=None
return 3:  3->2->1
```

Each node is visited once: O(n) time, O(1) space.

### Recursive reversal

```python
def reverse_rec(head):
    if head is None or head.next is None:
        return head
    new_head = reverse_rec(head.next)
    head.next.next = head  # flip
    head.next = None
    return new_head
```

It's elegant, but it uses **O(n) stack space**, one frame per node. In Python the default recursion limit is 1,000, so a 10,000-node list raises `RecursionError`. Prefer the loop.

## Fast and slow pointers

Move one pointer (`slow`) one step at a time and another (`fast`) two steps. The gap between them grows by one each step. That simple fact answers several questions in one pass.

### Finding the middle

When `fast` reaches the end, `slow` has gone half as far.

```python
def middle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    return slow
```

```
1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5
step 0: slow=1 fast=1
step 1: slow=2 fast=3
step 2: slow=3 fast=5  (stop)
middle = 3
```

For an even-length list such as `1..6`, this returns **4**, the second of the two middle nodes. If you need the first middle (useful for splitting a list in half for merge sort), use `while fast and fast.next and fast.next.next` to handle empty input too.

### Floyd's cycle detection

A bug or a malicious input can make a list loop back on itself. Walking it with `while cur:` then never ends. How do you detect a cycle?

The obvious answer is a set of visited nodes: O(n) time but **O(n) memory**. **Floyd's algorithm** (the "tortoise and hare") does it in O(1) memory.

If there's no cycle, `fast` falls off the end. If there is, both pointers end up circling the loop, and `fast` gains one node per step on `slow`, so it must eventually land exactly on it. It can't jump over `slow`: if `fast` is one behind, the next step brings them together.

```python
def has_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:
            return True
    return False
```

Note `is`: compare node *identity*, not values. Two different nodes can hold the same value.

### Finding where the cycle starts

Floyd's algorithm has a second phase. After the pointers meet, put one back at the head and advance **both one step at a time**. They meet again exactly at the first node of the cycle.

```python
def cycle_start(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:
            break
    else:
        return None        # no cycle
    p = head
    while p is not slow:
        p = p.next
        slow = slow.next
    return p
```

Why does that work? Let:

- **μ** = number of steps from the head to the cycle's start,
- **λ** = the cycle's length,
- **k** = how far into the cycle the pointers meet.

At the first positive-time meeting, slow has walked t = μ + k + jλ steps for some completed laps j ≥ 0, and fast has walked 2t. Their distance difference t is a multiple of λ, so μ + k is also a multiple of λ. This includes μ = 0, where the initial equality is not treated as a detected cycle.

So **μ ≡ −k (mod λ)**. A pointer starting at the meeting point (offset k) that walks μ more steps lands at offset k + μ = mλ, which is the cycle's start. A pointer walking μ steps from the head also lands there. Hence they meet at the start.

> [!example] Trace
> List `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6 -> (back to 3)`, so μ = 2 and λ = 4. Phase 1: slow visits 2, 3, 4, 5 while fast visits 3, 5, 3, 5. They meet at **5** after 4 steps (k = 2). Phase 2: starting from 1 and 5, one step each gives (2, 6), then (3, 3). They meet at **3**, the cycle start, after μ = 2 steps.

To get the cycle's length, hold one pointer at the meeting point and walk the other round until it returns, counting steps.

The same idea finds a duplicate in an array of n + 1 values in the range 1..n, treating each value as a "next" pointer. Brent's algorithm is a variant that typically does fewer pointer moves.

## Dummy heads

Many list operations treat the first node specially: deleting it changes `head`, and building a new list has no node to attach the first element to. A **dummy head** (a sentinel placed before the real head) removes the special case. Build or modify the list after the dummy, then return `dummy.next`.

### Removing the n-th node from the end

Use two pointers with a gap of n between them. When the front one hits the end, the back one is just before the target.

```python
def remove_nth_from_end(head, n):
    if not isinstance(n, int) or n < 1:
        raise ValueError("n must be >= 1")
    dummy = Node(0, head)
    front = back = dummy
    for _ in range(n + 1):
        if front is None:
            raise ValueError("n too large")
        front = front.next
    while front:
        front = front.next
        back = back.next
    back.next = back.next.next
    return dummy.next
```

Without the dummy, removing the *first* node (when n equals the length) needs its own branch. With it, `back` simply stays at the dummy and the general code works.

## Merging two sorted lists

Assume two sorted, acyclic, node-disjoint lists and constant-time value comparison. This destructive merge repeatedly takes the smaller head and attaches it to the result. A dummy head gives you somewhere to attach the first node.

```python
def merge(a, b):
    dummy = tail = Node(0)
    while a and b:
        if a.val <= b.val:
            tail.next, a = a, a.next
        else:
            tail.next, b = b, b.next
        tail = tail.next
    tail.next = a or b   # leftovers
    return dummy.next
```

```
a: 1 -> 4 -> 6
b: 2 -> 3 -> 7
take 1(a) 2(b) 3(b) 4(a) 6(a)
a empty: attach rest of b (7)
result: 1 2 3 4 6 7
```

This is O(n + m) time and O(1) extra space: it relinks existing nodes rather than creating new ones. Using `<=` keeps equal elements in their original order (a **stable** merge), which matters for merge sort.

Merge is the core of **merge sort on linked lists**, which is the standard way to sort a list in O(n log n) without random access: find the middle with fast/slow pointers, split, sort each half, merge.

## Combining patterns

Harder problems chain these together.

- **Is the list a palindrome, in O(1) space?** Find the middle (fast/slow), reverse the second half, compare the two halves node by node, then reverse it back to restore the list.
- **Reorder `1,2,3,4,5` to `1,5,2,4,3`?** Find the middle, reverse the second half, then interleave the halves.
- **Where do two lists intersect?** Walk pointer A along list A then list B, and pointer B along B then A. Both travel the same total distance, so they arrive at the shared node together (or both reach `None`).

> [!warning] Common bugs
> - Losing the rest of the list by overwriting `next` before saving it.
> - Checking `fast.next.next` without first checking `fast.next`, causing an AttributeError on short lists.
> - Comparing values (`==`) when you mean identity (`is`).
> - Forgetting to restore a list you mutated (for example in the palindrome check), surprising the caller.

## Key takeaways
- Iterative reversal uses `prev`, `cur` and a saved `nxt`: O(n) time, O(1) space. The recursive version uses O(n) stack.
- Fast/slow pointers find the middle in one pass, and detect cycles in O(1) memory (Floyd).
- After Floyd's pointers meet, restart one at the head and step both by one: they meet at the cycle start because μ + k is a multiple of λ.
- A dummy head removes head-of-list special cases in deletion and in building new lists.
- Merging two sorted lists is O(n + m) and stable with `<=`; it's the heart of linked-list merge sort.
